Where the data comes from

NASA GISS GISTEMP v4[1][2] combines land and ocean observations on a 2° grid with 1,200 km smoothing. Temperature anomalies use NASA’s 1951–1980 baseline. Grid values describe a broad area, so a city label is a shortcut to its grid cell.

GPCP v2.3[3] satellite and gauge precipitation is provided by NOAA PSL on a 2.5° grid. Each cell’s precipitation anomaly is the change in mean daily precipitation relative to its own 1991–2020 average.

NOAA ERSST v6[4] reconstructs sea surface temperatures from marine observations. NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1[5] combines observations with a weather model to estimate air and surface temperature, pressure, water vapor, wind, clouds, soil conditions, surface heat flux, and radiation. The reanalysis stopped in 2026, and changes in the observing network can affect trends.

NOAA OISST v2[6] provides the monthly sea ice concentration archive. The atlas uses complete years through 2022. Soil moisture and sea ice anomalies are measured in percentage points.

Monthly, seasonal, and annual anomalies

Monthly anomalies compare the selected month with that same month in the reference period. Seasonal and annual means weight each month by its number of days and require every month in the period. Dec–Feb is labeled by the January and February year, so Dec–Feb 2025 starts in December 2024. The timeline steps through consecutive periods. Select two points on the location chart to compare their anomalies. The change is the end value minus the start value. The location chart follows the selected month or season across years.

NASA GISTEMP supplies monthly anomalies relative to 1951–1980. For the other layers, the atlas subtracts the cell’s 1991–2020 average for the matching period. Missing cells appear in gray. Resampled layers use the nearest grid point, and the map keeps a fixed color scale across years within each view.

Historical averages

The inspector shows two averages for each selected grid cell and period. The baseline is the mean of the 30 values in 1991–2020 for the matching month, season, or year. Atlas reads it from the same source files and grid points used to calculate the anomalies. Percentage baselines are shown in percent, with their anomalies in percentage points. Temperatures supplied in kelvin are converted to Celsius for the baseline display.

For GISTEMP, NASA publishes departures from the 1951–1980 reference. The baseline shown is zero on that anomaly scale. NASA’s explanation of absolute temperature

The record average takes the arithmetic mean of the available historical anomalies for the selected period. Atlas shows the first and last available years and the number of values used. The average excludes missing values and projections, even when the timeline shows a projected date.

Comparing two places

Atlas subtracts B from A using the selected layer, year, and period for both cells. Each anomaly is relative to that cell’s own baseline. In the 30-year trend view the difference is between slopes ending in the selected year, expressed per decade. The side-by-side historical rates use the same 30 measured years when both cells have a complete window. The confidence interval and significance test in the inspector apply to the primary cell only.

For a projected date, the location panel compares the central estimates from the two cells. The chart shows a prediction range for the primary cell when available. The map shows one possible year, so map hover values can differ from the panel. The difference is unavailable when either cell lacks a value.

How trends are tested

The trend is the least squares slope across 30 consecutive years for the period shown. The trend map uses annual values. The location panel uses the chosen month or season when a shorter period is selected. Slopes are expressed per decade. The confidence interval and two-sided p-value use a Newey–West[7] standard error with three annual lags and an approximate normal reference distribution. The map colors represent slope magnitude. Each significance test applies to a single cell, without adjustment for multiple comparisons. The interval describes regression uncertainty and excludes uncertainty in the input dataset.

Projected years

The timeline continues past the last measured year to 2100, in violet. Formulas, the hindcast table, and limits are on the projections page.

Downloads and precision

The location panel exports the measured series, the fitted trend line, and the projection as CSV, the fit statistics as JSON, and the chart and map as PNG images. Each file names the source dataset. To keep downloads small, grids are stored as 16-bit integers with a step of about 0.002 in the layer’s unit (up to 0.009 W/m² for sensible heat flux), far below the uncertainty of the data. For full precision, use the original files linked under “Where this data comes from” on the atlas page.
